papers.title: Its the Art of Listening": Patient and Practitioner Perspectives on Acute Cardiac Care for Patients with a Severe Mental Illness (SMI): A Qualitative Interview Study
papers.abstract: Background: Patients with a severe mental illness experience disparities in acute cardiac care, yet reasons underlying these inequities remain poorly understood. We aimed to explore patient and healthcare professional perspectives of acute cardiac care to identify factors influencing care quality and equity. Methods and results: We conducted semi-structured videocall interviews with people with a severe mental illness who had been hospitalised following a myocardial infarction, and with Cardiology and Emergency Room healthcare professionals involved in acute cardiac care across two central Scottish health boards between July 2023 and April 2024. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis in NVivo. We conducted 21 interviews (13 healthcare professionals; 8 people with a severe mental illness). Although many patients reported empathic and supportive care, barriers were described. We identified 3 themes from the data: positive care experiences; cross-cutting care barriers, and challenges along the care pathway. Healthcare professionals sought to provide equitable care but reported challenges related to limited mental health training, diagnostic uncertainty, behavioural management and difficulties accessing psychiatric expertise, prescribed medication and associated information. Patients described experiences of stigma, communication difficulties, disruptions to psychiatric medication continuity and distress associated with overstimulating hospital environments. System-level barriers included staff shortages, limited access to liaison psychiatry, lack of clear care protocols and difficulties integrating mental and physical healthcare. Positive experiences were associated with empathic staff, feeling listened to, clear communication, and tailored efforts to create psychologically safe care environments. Conclusion: Inequities in acute cardiac care for people with a severe mental illness appear to arise from the interaction of patient complexity, clinician uncertainty and organisational constraints. Improving care will require greater integration of mental and physical health services, continuity of psychiatric treatment, psychologically-informed care environments, and support for staff delivering care to this complex patient group.

papers.title: Multilevel Interventions to Improve Colonoscopy Completion After Abnormal Fecal Immunochemical Testing in a Safety-Net Health System: Preliminary Findings from the IMPACTT Study
papers.abstract: Background: Timely diagnostic colonoscopy is a critical step after an abnormal fecal immunochemical test (FIT), yet many patients do not complete follow-up within recommended timeframes, particularly in safety-net settings. Barriers occur across multiple levels and stages of care, suggesting a need for interventions that address both clinic processes and patient-level barriers. Methods: IMProving Adherence to Colonoscopy through Teams and Technology (IMPACTT) evaluated two concurrent interventions across 12 adult primary care clinics in the San Francisco Health Network. A clinic-level Best Practice Bundle (BPB), implemented in a stepped-wedge rollout, included patient tracking, standardized electronic health record documentation, standardized education and communication, and audit and feedback. In parallel, we randomly assigned eligible patients to a patient-level instruction and navigation (PIN) intervention or usual care. PIN provided targeted outreach to patients who were neither referred nor scheduled, as well as multilingual text reminders that allowed patients to confirm, cancel, or reschedule their colonoscopy. The primary outcome was colonoscopy completion within 180 days of an abnormal FIT. This preliminary analysis reports unadjusted comparisons among patients with sufficient follow-up at the data cutoff. Results: Among 2,303 patients with an abnormal FIT, 1,136 were identified before and 1,167 after their clinic implemented the BPB. Colonoscopy completion within 180 days was 44.1% before BPB implementation and 60.1% after implementation (risk difference, 16.0 percentage points; 95% CI, 11.8 to 20.1; p<0.001). Referral to gastroenterology within 42 days increased from 69.8% to 84.2%, and among patients who completed colonoscopy, the median time from FIT to colonoscopy decreased from 131 to 86 days. In the randomized PIN trial, we assigned 1,415 patients to usual care (n=698) or PIN (n=717). Colonoscopy completion within 180 days did not differ between usual care and PIN (58.4% vs 57.7%; risk difference, -0.7 percentage points; 95% CI, -5.9 to 4.6; p=0.9). PIN also did not improve referral within 42 days or scheduling within 56 days. Conclusions: In preliminary unadjusted analyses, implementation of a clinic-level bundle targeting tracking, communication, documentation, and feedback was associated with improved timely follow-up after abnormal FIT, whereas a randomized technology-supported patient instruction and navigation intervention did not improve colonoscopy completion. Prespecified analyses accounting for calendar time, clinic-level clustering, patient characteristics, and concurrent intervention assignment are forthcoming. Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06191185.

papers.title: Human-centered design can optimize operational details of an implementation strategy: Experiences from a peer-based hypertension medication delivery program in western Kenya
papers.abstract: Background: Human-centered design (HCD) is a co-creation approach that is increasingly being utilized by implementation science researchers to engage key stakeholders in developing contextually appropriate health interventions and implementation strategies. The exact role of HCD in implementation research, however, remains uncertain. We describe the process, outcome, and experiences of using HCD to develop the operational details of an implementation strategy based on a pre-existing scaffolding that consisted of combining community-based peer medication delivery with health information technology (HIT) to improve medication adherence among hypertension patients in rural western Kenya. Methods: A design team of 22 members was formed representing key stakeholders: hypertension patients, healthcare workers, pharmacists, peers, HIT personnel, policy/program leaders, and implementation researchers. We conducted six meetings utilizing established HCD principles and processes (inspiration, brainstorming, conceptualization, creation, iteration, and finalization), aimed at developing a final implementation strategy with full operational details. Quantitative assessment of acceptability and appropriateness was conducted among healthcare workers, patients, and peers, using the Acceptability of Intervention Measure and Intervention Appropriateness Measure. Results: The design team developed key operational details across five domains: peer recruitment, training and monitoring; HIT; medication delivery; medication payment; and stakeholder identification. Acceptability and appropriateness scores (maximum of 20) were favorable among all participants, but mean scores were notably higher among patients with hypertension (19.3, 19.2) and peers (19.2, 19.2) compared to healthcare workers (17.7, 17.3). Specific recommendations were made to improve the acceptability and appropriateness of the strategy. These findings were subsequently used to develop a final iteration of the implementation strategy. Conclusion: HCD was feasible and useful in optimizing the operational details of our implementation strategy, aligning it with the healthcare goals and needs of the community. It allowed end-users to co-create with researchers, ultimately yielding high pre-implementation acceptability and appropriateness, which we anticipate will ultimately enhance implementation success.

papers.title: Exploring Perspectives of Healthcare Staff on Achieving the Healthcare Quality Standards in District Hospitals in Rwanda: A qualitative Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe World Health Organization (WHO) has recommended that quality of care (QoC) should be timely delivered within safe conditions based on patients needs and preferences. However, low- and middle-income countries face challenges such as understaffing and inadequate infrastructure, resulting in poor QoC. In 2012, Rwanda leveraged the pre-existing performance-based financing (PBF) to introduce continuous quality improvement (QI) towards accreditation recognition of district hospitals (DH). Despite these efforts, no DHs accredited by 2022. ObjectiveTo explore healthcare professionals (HCP) perspectives on achieving the delivery of standard QoC in Rwandan DHs. MethodsUsing an interpretative epistemology, this qualitative study conducted in-depth semi-structured interviews with 14 participants purposively sampled HCPs from Masaka (urban) and Remera-Rukoma (rural) DHs. Interview data were audio-recorded, manually transcribed, and analyzed with thematic content analysis. ResultsThe analysis revealed three main themes: perceptions about continuous QI towards accreditation recognition, barriers to achieving accreditation, and strategies to achieve the recognition. Participants from both hospitals expressed that the accreditation program required more efforts than the PBF approach. They also highlighted that the DHs were still at the awareness stage and had not clearly implemented the quality standards due to challenges such as low staff involvement and motivation, staff turnover and shortage, and limited budget for accreditation. Recommended strategies to achieve the recognition included staff motivation through increased incentives and salaries, cascaded accreditation rollout, integrating accreditation program into pre-service curriculum. ConclusionsThis qualitative study highlighted the challenges, such as limited budget and low staff motivation, impeding progress towards DH accreditation recognition. Cascaded accreditation rollout, enhanced staff incentives and salaries, and integration of accreditation program into pre-service curriculum were key strategies suggested for Rwanda Ministry of Health and DHs to achieve the required quality standards and recognition.

papers.title: Reducing Biosecurity Risks in Informal Poultry Slaughter: A Pilot Intervention Among Mobile Poultry Vendors in Bangladesh
papers.abstract: IntroductionMobile poultry vending and slaughtering practices in Bangladesh pose potential public health risks due to poor hygiene, unsafe waste disposal, and close human-animal interactions. Limited data exist on these practices and feasible interventions to improve biosecurity among mobile poultry vendors. MethodsThis mixed-method study was conducted in three phases across four sub-districts in three districts. Phase 1 involved 416 hours of structured observation, 40 in-depth vendor interviews, and 40 informal customer interviews. Phase 2 involved the development and pilot testing of an intervention package, including poultry killing cones, hand sanitizers, disinfectants, and a hygiene pamphlet, with 10 vendors. Phase 3 implemented the intervention among 20 vendors for one month, followed by 94 hours of observation and 17 customer interviews. ResultPhase 1 found 1,959 slaughtering events with no use of personal protective equipment; slaughtering occurred in plastic jars (58%), directly on roads (21%), and roadside drains (11%). Seventy percent of vendors reported discarding slaughtering waste directly into the environment, while 78% reported not knowing how poultry diseases could spread to other animals or humans. During Phase 2, 9/10 vendors considered the killing cone useful, although bicycle users reported challenges related to weight and balance; the cone was subsequently modified. During Phase 3, 294 poultry were observed being slaughtered, with 79% using killing cones. Waste was stored in cone-attached boxes in 97% of cone uses, and vendors used hand sanitizer before eating in 75% of observed instances. Among 17 interviewed customers, 88% recognized the cones role in safer waste disposal and 53% considered it useful overall. ConclusionThis study highlights major hygiene and biosecurity gaps and demonstrates that low-cost, targeted interventions may improve biosecurity practices among mobile poultry vendors and reduce opportunities for environmental contamination in informal slaughter settings.

papers.title: Large Language Model-Enhanced Electronic Frailty Assessment and Prognostic Performance in Hospitalized Adults: A Retrospective Cohort Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundElectronic frailty indices (eFIs) derived from structured electronic health record (EHR) data may incompletely capture functional deficits. Large language models (LLMs) can extract frailty-related information from clinical notes, but whether improved frailty ascertainment improves prognostic performance is uncertain. ObjectiveTo compare frailty ascertainment and prognostic performance between standard and LLM-enhanced eFIs among hospitalized adults. DesignRetrospective cohort study ParticipantsAdults aged [≥]50 years enrolled in two studies at an academic medical center and affiliated community hospital between February 2022 and April 2024. Main MeasuresA validated 35-deficit diagnosis-based eFI and an LLM-enhanced eFI incorporating deficits extracted from physical therapy (PT) documentation using GPT-4o. Frailty was defined using an index threshold of [≥]0.20. The primary outcome was a composite of discharge to a facility, readmission, or death within 90 days. Multivariable logistic regression models assessed associations with the outcome, and discrimination was compared using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). Secondary analyses examined threshold-based classification and PT-documentation availability; prespecified sensitivity analyses evaluated population and outcome restrictions. ResultsAmong 616 hospitalizations, mean (SD) age was 70.9 (10.2) years, 329 (53.4%) had PT documentation, and 320 (51.9%) experienced the composite outcome. Standard and LLM-enhanced eFIs classified 216 (35.1%) and 362 (58.8%) hospitalizations as frail, respectively. Both were independently associated with the outcome (standard eFI: adjusted OR, 1.98 [95% CI, 1.39-2.83]; LLM-enhanced eFI: adjusted OR, 2.46 [95% CI, 1.75-3.47]). Discrimination did not differ significantly (AUROC, 0.636 vs 0.660; difference, 0.024 [95% CI, -0.006 to 0.053]; p=0.12). LLM enhancement increased sensitivity (42.5% to 69.4%) but decreased specificity (73.0% to 52.7%). ConclusionsLLM enhancement substantially increased frailty ascertainment and sensitivity for adverse outcomes but did not significantly improve prognostic discrimination. Thus, LLM-enhanced frailty assessment may depend on whether the intended use prioritizes broad identification of functional vulnerability or prediction of adverse post-hospital outcomes.

papers.title: An Edge-AI Pose-Estimation Platform for Real-Time Posture and Posture-Transition Monitoring: A Feasibility Study for Pre-Emptive Fall-Risk Alerting in Elderly and Dementia Care
papers.abstract: Falls and unmonitored patient movements remain leading causes of harm in healthcare settings. Current solutions - such as weight-based alarms, remote video monitoring, and in-person sitters - are reactive, labor-intensive, or prone to false alarms, often compromising both care quality and staff efficiency. We developed a machine learning-enabled, proactive-preventive patient monitoring platform that uses 17-keypoint pose estimation to detect changes in patient posture and generate alerts in real time. The Edge-AI device integrates a Raspberry Pi 5, Hailo-8L neural processing unit (NPU), and Raspberry Pi camera module 3, and runs Hailo-YOLOv8-Pose at 30 frames per second to classify postures (i.e., lying, Fowlers, sitting, standing). Alerts are transmitted via Bluetooth to caregivers through earphones or speakers. System performance was evaluated across multiple scenarios, including bed and chair monitoring, free limb movement, partial body occlusion (e.g., blankets), and varying lighting and care environments. The platform maintained accurate monitoring under varying lighting conditions, including lights-off scenarios, and because all processing occurs locally without network dependence, it is designed to continue operating during network outages - an important resilience feature for care environments where connectivity may be interrupted. By abstracting images into skeletal keypoints without recording video, the system preserves privacy while potentially enabling earlier intervention and reducing false alarms and caregiver workload. This cost-effective, scalable system supports future enhancements such as dual alerting, multi-device full-room coverage, and continuous monitoring for dementia patients.

papers.title: Impact of a hospital digital coordination centre on patient flow in a large tertiary centre
papers.abstract: Hospitals globally are under increasing strain due to rising demand and constrained capacity. This interrupted-time-series study evaluates the impact of a digital coordination centre, implemented on 28 August 2023, where a multidisciplinary operational team (comprising data scientists, patient flow managers, facilities managers, patient transport and nursing staff, for example) use real-time data dashboards showing measures of emergency department (ED) crowding and inpatient utilisation to optimise patient flow in an Australian metropolitan tertiary hospital. Analysis of 195,385 emergency department arrivals admitted to acute care and 184,454 acute inpatient episodes between July 2020 and June 2025 showed substantial improvements in measures of patient flow: 33% decrease in ED length of stay, 73% increase in hospital admissions from the ED within four hours of arrival, 8% decrease in inpatient length of stay, and 5% increase in discharges completed before noon. These changes coincided with a broader programme of organisational and operational reform, of which the DCC was a central integrating component. Hence, the findings support digitally enabled coordination centres as an effective contribution to the overall strategy for improving hospital operational efficiency.

papers.title: Using Vision and Large Language Models for Psychological Intervention Competency Assessment: A Pilot Study of Agreement with Clinician Ratings
papers.abstract: Introduction: Supervision in psychological intervention training is limited by the time needed to evaluate simulated sessions. We tested a Vision Language Model (VLM) and Large Language Model (LLM) pipeline that assesses competency from verbal and nonverbal communication. Method: Gemini-3.1-Pro was used to annotate behaviors in 25 simulated therapy videos and incorporate them into transcripts, and ChatGPT-6.1-Sol rated them against the ENACT scale. Two clinicians verified VLM-identified behaviors and four independently rated each video. Agreement was estimated with Gwet's AC1 and ICC. Results: Of 1,558 VLM-identified behaviors, 70% were confirmed by both clinicians and 93% by at least one. AI-clinician agreement on therapeutic behavior attributes (AC1=0.73, 95% CI 0.70-0.76) approached between-clinician agreement (0.75, 0.72-0.78). AI-clinician ICCs on therapeutic domain levels (median 0.57) were modestly lower than between-clinician ICCs (0.67). Discussion: The pipeline agreed with clinicians nearly as well as clinicians agreed with each other and shows promise as a supplementary evaluator in therapist training.

papers.title: Clinical Prediction Model Performance Metrics Cluster at Arbitrary Thresholds and are Incorrectly Reported in High-Ranking Journals: An Observational Meta-Research Study
papers.abstract: Background Previous research has shown that clinical prediction models have likely been 'hacked' to meet arbitrary performance thresholds. However, this work only assessed abstracts, could not identify models with a perfect AUC (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve) of 1, and did not examine other performance metrics. Methods We collected data from full texts and validated a large language model to extract data from a random sample of Q1 journal articles for 2025. We examined if hacking occurred in the AUC value, sensitivity and specificity, and checked if articles correctly reported the AUC value from corresponding receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves. Results We identified 2,001 prediction model articles that reported 15,656 AUC values. We found a striking excess of results near perfect prediction and at multiples of five and ten for the AUC, sensitivity and specificity, indicating likely manipulated data, methods or publication bias. Around 1 in 40 AUC values were reported outside of their confidence intervals, and around 1 in 8 ROC curves did not match their reported AUC value. Conclusion We have shown that not only the AUC value, but the sensitivity and specificity are being hacked, likely to help the authors publish their paper at the cost of evidence for practice. Excess models that are not representative of their true performance may misguide clinicians, distort the literature, and make it harder to find prediction models that are useful for practice.

papers.title: Keeping care alive in 2025-26 humanitarian Somalia: routine digital data and frontline and managerial perspectives on integrated services
papers.abstract: In conflict-affected settings facing polycrisis and a contraction in humanitarian funding, service integration helps sustain care with fewer resources, yet lacks a simple measure. We examine how the Caafimaad+ consortiums vaccination, nutrition, and mental health services functioned under pressure in Somalia in 2025-2026. Using the Levesque conceptual framework with a sequential mixed-methods approach, we organised participatory workshops with 21 frontline workers, then nine managers, from nine structures around Mogadishu area in November-December 2025. We built an integration indicator from routine data for six structures (April 2025-March 2026). Workers described continuous pressure worsened by US funding cuts and ranked supply availability as most critical dimension. Facilities kept running through constant adaptations and informal mechanisms, especially smaller facilities. Vaccination-to-nutrition integration rate declined significantly, reflecting a dilution effect. The nutrition-to-vaccination rate showed a similar trend but non-significant. The fall in nutrition contacts matched supply shortage reports. This low-cost, reproducible approach refine service-volume monitoring where data collection is risky. Finally, our study identified a second, overlooked group: the frontline workers themselves. They sustain services through their informal efforts, but at the expense of their own well-being.

papers.title: What successful adaptation reveals about capability and dependence in healthcare: A Brittle Threshold perspective
papers.abstract: Healthcare teams routinely adapt to changing demands by redistributing tasks, stretching roles, and reorganizing coordination. Although these adjustments can sustain performance, their immediate success provides limited insight into how they affect the conditions supporting subsequent adaptation. We examined how successful adaptation reorganizes collective work and what these changes might reveal about emerging limits to adaptability. Guided by Brittle Threshold as a sensitizing concept, we conducted a secondary qualitative analysis of 34 anonymized interviews from four studies involving hospital teams during COVID-19, military surgical resuscitation teams, rural emergency care teams, and a community-led mass vaccination initiative. The datasets provided accounts of adaptation under varied demands and constraints. Across settings, adaptation changed collective work through four connected domains: work redistribution, coordination reconfiguration, responsibility concentration, and human requirements. Similar adaptations were sustained under different conditions. Some were accompanied by shared learning, expanded skills, and alternative sources of support, while others maintained performance through continued dependence on particular individuals, restricted access, or sustained personal effort. These patterns could coexist within the same setting. Examining the relationships among the four domains revealed differences in how collective performance was organized and supported that were not apparent from successful task completion alone. The findings offer an empirically grounded approach to examining potential Brittle Threshold signals in everyday healthcare work. Rather than identifying particular adaptive behaviours as warning signs, they direct attention to changing configurations of responsibility, coordination, support, and human effort. This perspective can inform investigations of how healthcare teams sustain adaptability as demands change.

papers.title: Are Longer Waits Associated with Lower Satisfaction and Worse Recovery? A Retrospective Observational Study of Hip and Knee Replacement in England
papers.abstract: ObjectivesTo examine whether longer waits for hip and knee replacement were associated with higher post-operative patient dissatisfaction and smaller patient-reported functional improvement, and whether worse post-operative satisfaction was associated with smaller functional improvement, in National Health Service (NHS) care in England. DesignRetrospective observational study linking respondent-level Patient Reported Outcome Measures (PROMs) to provider-year Referral to Treatment (RTT) waiting times, with a supplementary comparison of the wait-dissatisfaction relationship in general practice. SettingNHS-funded hip and knee replacement in England, 2017, 2018, 2022 and 2023, excluding the pandemic-affected years 2019-2021. Participants107,700 hip and 122,756 knee replacement PROMs respondents, and all 42 Integrated Care Boards (168 ICB-year observations) for the general practice comparison. Primary and Secondary Outcome MeasuresPost-operative dissatisfaction (fair or poor on a five-point satisfaction scale) and Oxford Score improvement (post-operative minus pre-operative score). Secondary outcomes were EO-5D improvement and the full five-category satisfaction score. ResultsEach additional 30 days of average wait was associated with a 0.05 increase in the log-odds of post-operative dissatisfaction for hip (95% CI 0.03 to 0.08) and 0.04 for knee (0.03 to 0.06), and with smaller Oxford Score improvement (hip -0.26 points, -0.44 to -0.08; knee -0.11 points, -0.22 to -0.01). Mean Oxford Score improvement fell monotonically across satisfaction categories, from 26.11 points (hip) and 22.74 points (knee) among patients reporting excellent satisfaction to 2.62 and -0.01 points among those reporting poor satisfaction. In general practice, the wait-dissatisfaction association was close to zero but too imprecise to rule out an association of the size seen for hip and knee replacement. ConclusionsIn this focused surgical pathway, waiting times, post-operative satisfaction and patient-reported recovery were consistently associated, and satisfaction carried information about patient-reported recovery, not only about the experience of care. Performance frameworks that apply a common satisfaction measure across care settings should not assume it carries the same outcome content in each. Strengths and Limitations of this StudyO_LIRespondent-level national PROMs data observed waiting time, post-operative satisfaction and a validated functional outcome (Oxford Score) for the same 107,700 hip and 122,756 knee replacement patients. C_LIO_LITwo wait exposures, average wait and share of pathways completed after 18 weeks, were each adjusted for comorbidities and fixed effects, with ordered logit and EO-5D analyses as robustness checks. C_LIO_LIThe wait exposure is a provider-year average across the whole trauma and orthopaedics treatment function, so it proxies rather than measures the procedure-specific wait. C_LIO_LICase mix was adjusted only through 12 comorbidity flags; patient age and sex were not available in the PROMs extract. C_LIO_LIThe design is observational, and because satisfaction is reported after recovery, the direction of the satisfaction-recovery association cannot be established. C_LI

papers.title: Associations between patient characteristics at referral and social worker care coordinator allocation in mental healthcare: a retrospective cohort study.
papers.abstract: ObjectivesTo investigate care coordination delivered specifically by social workers and, more generally, by other professionals using electronic health records. Study design and SettingA retrospective cohort study in a large mental healthcare provider serving a South London catchment. SampleThe study comprised care coordination episodes from 2007-2023 for adults aged 18-65 years at the time of commencement. We categorised these by the care coordinators profession: social worker, nurse, doctor, and others, with a focus in the analysis on social worker care coordination. In addition to sociodemographic data, we obtained diagnosis, mental health service use, and symptoms over the 12 months preceding episode start. Outcome measuresSocial workers associations with mental healthcare service use 12 months before the episode start. Cases allocated to social workers the year after had higher rates across most service-use outcomes. ResultsOf 327,056 care coordination episodes for 132,553 patients, 10.6% had a social worker care coordinator. Full-adjusted associations with social worker care coordinator included longer duration since first referral (IRR 1.05, 95% CI 1.03-1.07, P <0.001), more prior hospitalisations involving compulsory detention (1.11, 1.07-1.15, P <0.001), more days under a home treatment team (1.25, 1.17-1.34, P <0.001), and more emergency department mental health contacts (1.10, 1.07-1.14, P <0.001), as well as higher recorded symptoms on all scales. ConclusionEpisodes with social workers as care coordinators are associated with more complex needs, severe symptoms and a later stage in the course of care. The assignment of care coordinators by profession and its influence on clinical outcomes remain unclear; further mixed-methods research could help clarify this. Article SummaryO_ST_ABSStrengths and limitations of this studyC_ST_ABSO_LIWe believe this is the first large quantitative study evaluating the care coordination delivered by social workers specifically or between different professional groups. C_LIO_LIThe study incorporates an evaluation of symptom profiles utilising natural language processing. C_LIO_LIOur study utilised a large sample from routine mental healthcare over a long period from a highly socially and culturally diverse catchment. C_LIO_LIThis study from a single catchment and provider. C_LIO_LIComparisons relied on the assigning of a profession to each care coordinator. C_LI

papers.title: Heat and Emergency Department Operations: A Two-Decade Observational Study
papers.abstract: Emergency department (ED) crowding remains one of the most pressing challenges facing the US healthcare system; environmental factors have received little attention as determinants of ED operational performance, patient behavior, or emergency service utilization. We examined the association between maximum daily heat index and ED throughput metrics, patient behavioral outcomes, and likelihood of EMS arrival. We retrospectively analyzed 485,403 warm-season ED visits from a 22-year period at a large urban academic medical center in New England. The exposure was daily maximum heat index (ERA5-Land) for Suffolk County, Massachusetts. Primary outcomes included four ED throughput time metrics: door-to-doctor time, doctor-to-decision time, boarding time, and total ED length of stay; secondary outcomes included the left without being seen rate, leaving against medical advice rate, and likelihood of EMS arrival. Each 1{degrees}F increase in heat index was associated with a 0.41% increase in door-to-doctor time (95% CI: 0.38% - 0.44%). Heat index was not significantly associated with the other three throughput metrics. At the 95{degrees}F heat index threshold, patients were 27% more likely to leave against medical advice than on days below the threshold (OR 1.27; 95% CI: 1.02 - 1.58), and had higher odds of arriving by EMS (OR 1.10; 95% CI: 1.06 - 1.15). Higher heat index was associated with longer door-to-doctor time, increased EMS arrival proportion, and higher odds of leaving against medical advice. Health systems and municipalities should characterize how hot weather affects operational performance and integrate this evidence into heat-readiness planning.

papers.title: Development and Psychometric Evaluation of the AASPIRE Social Support Scale for Autistic Adults
papers.abstract: BackgroundSocial support is associated with health, well-being, and quality of life among autistic adults, yet existing social support measures have important limitations. Many were not developed with autistic people, may be difficult for autistic adults to use, and have limited psychometric evidence in autistic populations. We evaluated the psychometric properties of the AASPIRE Social Support Scale, an autism-informed measure adapted from Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) social support scales through a community-based participatory research process. MethodsThe AASPIRE Social Support Scale assesses five domains: Companionship, Emotional Support, Informational Support, Practical Support, and Social Isolation. Baseline data were analyzed from 859 autistic adults recruited through healthcare systems, disability service systems, and the broader U.S. autism community. Participants completed the measure independently (n=600), with support (n=189), or through caregiver report (n=70). We evaluated content validity, structural validity using confirmatory factor analysis, internal consistency, and measurement invariance across reporting approaches. We also explored differences in social support scores by reporting approach and participant characteristics. ResultsThe hypothesized five-factor structure demonstrated good fit, with strong item loadings supporting the five distinct but related social support domains. Internal consistency was high for the total scale and all subscales (Cronbachs =.87-.95). Measurement invariance was supported across independent direct-report, supported direct-report, and caregiver report, indicating that the scale measured the underlying social support domains similarly across reporting approaches. Social support scores differed across reporting groups: participants reporting independently generally reported less support and greater isolation than participants completing the measure with support or through caregiver report. Exploratory analyses also identified differences by age and gender, but not race. ConclusionsThe AASPIRE Social Support Scale is an accessible, reliable, and valid multidimensional measure of social support for autistic adults. Its comparable measurement properties across independent direct-report, supported direct-report, and caregiver report support its use in studies seeking to include autistic adults with diverse communication and support needs. The scale may be useful for evaluating social support and the effectiveness of services and interventions across heterogeneous autistic adult populations.

papers.title: Where did it go? How Information Management Practices Impact Rigor and Reproducibility in Collaborative Clinical and Translational Research
papers.abstract: IntroducationClinical and translational research teams (CTRTs) use a vast array of information (digital artifacts used to generate, share, and retrieve data) in their collaborative work, yet information management is often devalued compared to more visible aspects of data-related work. In this second paper from the Information Management Prototype for Clinical and Translational Research (IMPACT-CTR) study, we present (1) the shared practices CTRT members implemented to manage, store, retrieve and share their information, and (2) the impact of these practices on the teams and their work. MethodsWe conducted individual semi-structured interviews with 52 team members across 11 CTRTs. ResultsWe identified information practices that spanned research activities such as team meetings, data collection, dissemination, and overall project management. Effective management of information fostered workflow efficiency, increased shared awareness, and built confidence in the research CTRTs produced. However, inconsistent management of information slowed the workflow, created frustration, and reduced trust in the completeness of research outputs. DiscussionThese results demonstrate that information practices are deeply interdependent, preserve institutional knowledge, and ultimately bolster the efficient and effective progression of scientific work. CTRTs who took time to reflect on, implement, and evaluate several lightweight practices through the research lifecycle enhanced the rigor and reproducibility of their science.

papers.title: Implementing an EHR-Integrated Quality and Safety Dashboard to Improve Inpatient Safety: Clinical Usage and Preliminary Outcomes
papers.abstract: BackgroundData driven tools are increasingly used to support patient safety and quality improvement, yet evidence on the impact of integrated quality and safety dashboards remains limited. MethodsWe conducted a pre-post implementation study using interrupted time series analysis to evaluate the impact of an EHR-integrated quality and safety dashboard on clinical processes and patient outcomes, among three general medicine units at a 171-bed community teaching hospital. All adult patients admitted during seven-month pre- and post-implementation periods were included. The primary outcome was the proportion of hospitalizations with at least one adverse event. Secondary and exploratory outcomes included hospital-acquired conditions, adherence to safety-related process measures, and dashboard utilization. ResultsA total of 9,023 hospitalizations were included (4,640 pre-implementation; 4,383 post-implementation). The proportion of hospitalizations with at least one adverse event was similar pre-implementation (23.15%; 95% CI, 20.96-25.29) and post-implementation (22.97%; 95% CI, 20.86-25.23). CLABSI per 100 patient-days was reduced (aOR 0.47, 95% CI [0.37-0.60]); and exploratory analyses demonstrated decreases in slope for post-discharge venous thromboembolism (aOR, 0.66; 95% CI, 0.48-0.91; p=0.01) and hospital-acquired pressure injury (aOR, 0.69; 95% CI, 0.48-1.00; p=0.05). Several process measures improved, including code status confirmation, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, delirium screening, chlorhexidine bathing, and fall precautions. ConclusionsImplementation of an EHR-integrated quality and safety dashboard was associated with meaningful improvements in multiple care processes and CLABSI but not overall adverse events. These findings highlight the potential of workflow-integrated dashboards to support frontline quality improvement, while underscoring the need for additional measures to improve clinical outcomes.

papers.title: Fragmented and Underutilized: Exploring Role Variation and Ambiguity for Research Project Managers in Collaborative Team Science
papers.abstract: IntroductionClinical and translational research (CTR) increasingly relies on collaborative and interdisciplinary research teams to translate discoveries into practical solutions. Research project managers (RPMs) often support CTR projects to ensure continual progress toward research goals, yet there is still ambiguity around what research project management is and the role RPMs play on research teams. Our study aimed to address this gap in knowledge by understanding how RPMs (1) define project management in an academic research context and (2) align on the key job responsibilities of RPMs. MethodsSurvey responses from 85 academic RPMs and 14 semi-structured follow-up interviews were analyzed to characterize their perspectives and experiences. ResultsFindings revealed four themes: (1) RPMs were in alignment with each other and the Project Management Institute on the definition of project management while noting distinctions between academic and industry contexts, (2) RPMs reported diverse job responsibilities despite having similar job titles, (3) RPMs struggled with role ambiguity stemming from variability in key job responsibilities, and (4) RPMs identified areas of support to improve research project management. DiscussionThese findings contribute to a greater understanding of project management in academic research contexts and highlight the variable utilization of RPMs on collaborative teams. Well managed projects rarely happen naturally, but can have a large impact on research environments, team member wellbeing, and overall research productivity. By characterizing how RPMs define and enact their role, this study provides a foundation for developing resources and avenues of support that can ultimately increase the efficiency of translating research discoveries from bench to bedside.

papers.title: Strengthening Childhood Cancer Care in Nepal (DECAN-CHILD): Protocol for Evaluating Quality, Financial Burden and Health System Readiness Through a Prospective Cohort Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundStrengthening health systems in low-and middle-income countries (LMICs) like Nepal is essential for equitable, high-quality diagnosis and treatment and improved survival from childhood cancer. This study aims to quantify care intervals and their determinants; assess the quality of care and 1-, 2-, and 3-year survival; quantify the costs and cost burden of childhood cancer treatment from family and health system perspectives; and to assess the capacity of health systems in Nepal to diagnose and treat children with cancer. MethodsThis three-year prospective cohort study will enrol and follow consecutive childhood cancer patients aged 0-19 years registered at six tertiary hospitals in Nepal, accounting for approximately 90% of childhood cancer cases diagnosed nationally. After obtaining informed consent and assent, a semi structured questionnaire will be administered to patient/caregiver at baseline and every three months during the first year and every six months in the second and third years. Patient/caregiver data will be supplemented with patients medical records kept in the hospital. A national capacity assessment will assess readiness for childhood cancer care in tertiary-level and secondary-level healthcare facilities involved in referral, diagnosis, treatment or shared care. Survival outcomes will be examined using Cox proportional hazards models and random effects models to account for hospital clustering. Out-of-pocket costs will be analysed using descriptive statistics and a two-part regression model to account for zero-inflated cost distributions, with five-year health system cost projections modelled to estimate corresponding rates of catastrophic health expenditure and medical impoverishment. DiscussionThis study will generate comprehensive evidence on childhood cancer care, costs, and health system capacity for care in Nepal. Findings will directly inform policy guidance, resource allocation and benefit package design for childhood cancer care in Nepal, inform comparable efforts in other low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), and will contribute to Nepals efforts in the WHO Global Initiative for Childhood Cancer towards improved cancer outcomes.

papers.title: From Evidence to Intervention: A Systematic, Multi-Stakeholder Approach to Developing and Prioritizing Diagnostic Excellence Interventions Across a 14-Site Hospital Medicine Collaborative
papers.abstract: BackgroundDiagnostic errors are common and represent a leading cause of preventable harm in hospitalized medical patients. Despite growing recognition of this problem, the field lacks a systematic, evidence-based approach for developing, adapting, and selecting diagnostic excellence interventions at scale across multiple institutions. MethodsUsing a structured, multi-phase process, the Achieving Diagnostic Excellence through Prevention and Teamwork (ADEPT) collaborative, a 14-site AHRQ-funded hospital medicine network: (1) conducted an environmental scan of existing diagnostic safety practices across sites; (2) constructed a conceptual framework organizing potential interventions by target (patient, provider/team, health system) and safety paradigm (Safety I and Safety II); (3) convened multidisciplinary working groups to develop detailed proposals for six intervention programs; (4) applied a pre-specified multi-criteria rubric to facilitate group deliberation, and (5) voted to select a single high-priority intervention for collaborative launch. ResultsSix interventions were developed, selected, or adapted from prior work, spanning all cells of the target and safety paradigm framework. Finalized proposals were then shared at two separate ADEPT meetings - the first to solicit feedback on interventions and to coordinate activities across groups, and the second where a formal ranked-choice vote was held. This process resulted in selection of the Diagnostic Cross-Check (DXC) -- a structured, peer second-opinion program triggered by rapid response team (RRT) events -- as the highest priority intervention for collaborative-wide launch. The remaining interventions were designated as components of an ADEPT toolbox for future adaptation, adoption, and evaluation. DiscussionThe ADEPT collaboratives systematic, evidence-informed approach to diagnostic intervention development offers a replicable model for other multi-site quality improvement networks. The resulting portfolio of interventions provides a roadmap for the field of inpatient diagnostic excellence.

papers.title: Pharmacist-Led Comprehensive Medication Management and Patient Outcomes in Pediatric Intensive Care Unit Patients: A Multicenter Cohort Study
papers.abstract: ObjectiveClinical pharmacists improve medication management and safety in intensive care units, yet their role in neonatal and pediatric intensive care remains highly variable across institutions. Evidence supporting standardized clinical pharmacy practice models in these settings is limited. This study evaluated the association between pharmacist service coverage and clinical outcomes in critically ill pediatric patients. DesignMulticenter, observational study with prospective and retrospective data collection. SettingICUs at participating institutions in the United States and internationally. PatientsPatients <18 years of age InterventionNone MeasurementsThe primary exposure was pharmacist-led comprehensive medication management (CMM) with daily participation in multidisciplinary rounds. The secondary exposure was the pharmacist-to-ICU-patient ratio. The primary outcome was hazard of discharge alive (HDA) from the ICU. Secondary outcomes included in-hospital mortality, hospital HDA, and hazard of extubation alive (HEA). Fine-Gray competing risks models and multivariable Firth logistic regression were used for adjusted analyses. Main resultsA total of 1,459 patients cared for by 69 clinical pharmacists across 31 institutions were included. Daily CMM with rounding was associated with a higher HDA from the ICU (HR 2.60, 95% CI 2.17-3.10; p<0.001), higher HDA from the hospital (HR 2.25, 95% CI 1.83-2.75; p<0.001), and a higher HEA (HR 1.21, 95% CI 1.10-1.33; p<0.001), but not with in-hospital mortality (OR 0.44, 95% CI 0.14-1.36; p=0.154). The pharmacist-to-ICU-patient ratio was not significantly associated with ICU HDA (HR 1.00, 95% CI 0.99-1.01; p=0.88) or any secondary outcome. ConclusionsDaily pharmacist-provided CMM with multidisciplinary ICU rounding was associated with improved discharge outcomes among critically ill pediatric and neonatal patients, whereas pharmacist-to-ICU-patient ratio alone was not. These findings support standardized integration of clinical pharmacists into daily multidisciplinary rounds in this setting.

papers.title: Emergency Department Utilization Following a Community Hospital Closure: A Population-Based Comparative Study
papers.abstract: ImportanceHospital closures may alter access to emergency care. However, changes in utilization among residents of affected communities are less well characterized than changes in volume at surrounding hospitals. ObjectiveTo compare changes in emergency department (ED) utilization among Madera County residents following the closure of Madera Community Hospital (MCH) with changes among Fresno County residents, and to examine geographic differences by pre-closure reliance on MCH. Design, Setting, and ParticipantsRetrospective population-based comparative study of annual California hospital Patient Origin/Market Share data, 2015-2024, with an exploratory comparative interrupted time-series analysis. Pre-pandemic years were 2015-2019, pandemic-affected pre-closure years were 2020-2022, and the two complete closure years were 2023-2024. Encounters were classified by county of patient residence, regardless of treating hospital location. Main Outcomes and MeasuresCombined ED encounters (ED-only plus inpatient-from-ED) and each component separately. County-level utilization was expressed as encounters per 1,000 residents using annual population estimates. Geographic comparisons by pre-closure MCH dependence used ZIP-code encounter counts. ResultsFrom 2022 to 2023, the first complete year following closure, combined ED utilization declined from 398.47 to 333.61 encounters per 1,000 Madera County residents (-16.3%), compared with 399.61 to 398.49 (-0.3%) among Fresno County residents. Madera ED-only rates declined 20.4%, while inpatient-from-ED rates increased 13.4%; however, the adjusted comparative analysis did not identify a consistent additional Madera-specific increase in inpatient-from-ED utilization. Exploratory regression estimated Madera-specific closure-period rate ratios of 0.871 for combined ED utilization and 0.848 for ED-only utilization. Combined ED encounter counts declined 18.4% in high-MCH-dependence ZIP codes versus 5.8% in low-dependence ZIP codes. Statistical inference was limited by the inclusion of only two counties, two complete closure years, and substantial overdispersion. Conclusions and RelevanceThe period following MCH closure was associated with a substantial reduction in ED utilization among Madera County residents relative to Fresno County residents, concentrated in ED-only encounters and communities previously most dependent on MCH. The observational design does not establish causation or determine whether reduced utilization reflected substitution to other care settings, decreased demand, or unmet medical need.

papers.title: Why Have Drug Names Become So Weird? A Retrospective Analysis of the Orthographic Distinctiveness of Proprietary and Generic Names Across Four Decades of FDA Approvals
papers.abstract: BackgroundRegulatory pressure to avoid confusingly similar drug names appears to have pushed manufacturers to coin more distinctive proprietary names, but no one has quantitatively analyzed this trend. ObjectiveTo determine whether proprietary drug names became more orthographically distinctive (unusual in spelling) over time. MethodsWe examined 1,321 US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) new molecular entity (NME) names (1985-2024), 2,769 FDA Orange Book trade names (1982-2026), 177,337 US pharmaceutical trademarks (1980-2026), and 1,273 generic names (1982-2025). Compared to prior names (including those already marketed) and ordinary English, we scored each names character trigram (three-letter sequence) surprisal (statistical unexpectedness) and its edit-distance similarity to the closest existing names. Linear regression tested time trends, controlling for name length. ResultsMean NME trigram surprisal rose in every decade between the 1980s and 2020s, from 7.21 to 8.50 nats (natural-logarithm units, higher meaning less predictable), an 18% increase (b = 0.038, p < .001, R{superscript 2} = 0.34). Half of 2020s names (7% in the 1980s) contained a letter sequence found in no common English word (e.g., Jesduvroq, Omvoh). Nearest-neighbor similarity fell after the early 1990s. Trademark data showed the same trend (b = 0.016, p < .001). Generic names showed a weaker trend (b = 0.011, R{superscript 2} = 0.063). ConclusionsOver four decades, drug names became more orthographically distinctive, consistent with namespace crowding, deliberate efforts to avoid confusing names, and branding strategy. Because unfamiliar letter sequences can introduce other error pathways, increased distinctiveness does not necessarily imply improved safety.

papers.title: Patient Perceptions of Student Involvement and Satisfaction in a Student-Run Free Clinic Serving People Experiencing Homelessness
papers.abstract: BackgroundPatient satisfaction is a key measure of healthcare quality among people experiencing homelessness. Student-run free clinics (SRFCs) provide care to underserved populations, but the role of student involvement in patient satisfaction remains unclear. MethodsWe conducted a cross-sectional study of patients receiving care at an SRFC. From February 2024 to February 2025, patients completed post-visit surveys assessing satisfaction that were evaluated using regression analyses. ResultsEighty-eight patients completed surveys, reporting high overall satisfaction (mean 9.26/10). In separate linear regression models adjusted for age, gender, and race, greater perceived benefit of student involvement was associated with higher satisfaction ({beta} = .298, p =.037), whereas perceiving the visit as too long was associated with lower satisfaction ({beta} = -.285, p = .019). ConclusionGreater perceived benefit of student involvement was associated with higher patient satisfaction, whereas longer perceived visit duration was associated with lower satisfaction. These findings highlight the importance of balancing educational opportunities with efficient workflows in SRFCs.

papers.title: Effect of a culturally adapted birth preparedness and complication readiness training intervention on knowledge among Hehe pregnant women in rural Iringa Tanzania: A controlled pretest-posttest quasi-experimental study
papers.abstract: BackgroundBirth preparedness and complication readiness (BPCR) knowledge is important for recognizing maternal and newborn danger signs and preparing for timely care. However, conventional translation of BPCR educational materials may not adequately address local linguistic and cultural contexts. This study evaluated whether a culturally adapted Swahili BPCR training manual improved knowledge more than a standard translated Swahili BPCR training manual among Hehe pregnant women in rural Iringa, Tanzania. MethodsA controlled pretest-posttest quasi-experimental study was conducted among 176 pregnant women attending antenatal care in Mufindi and Kilolo districts. Eighty-eight women received the Culturally Adapted Swahili BPCR Training Manual and 88 received the Standard Translated Swahili BPCR Training Manual. Both groups received comparable BPCR education with standardized session duration, delivery format, language, and follow-up procedures. BPCR knowledge was assessed using a 64-item questionnaire at baseline and four weeks after the intervention. The primary analysis used Difference-in-Differences regression to compare changes in knowledge between groups. Multiple linear regression was used to assess the association between intervention-group assignment and post-intervention knowledge after adjustment for baseline knowledge and participant characteristics. ResultsAll 176 participants completed both assessments. Mean knowledge scores increased from 21.01 (SD 7.42) to 38.49 (SD 7.54) in the culturally adapted group and from 22.51 (SD 5.80) to 32.81 (SD 5.55) in the standard translated group. The culturally adapted group demonstrated a 7.18-point greater increase in knowledge than the standard translated group ({beta} = 7.18, 95% CI: 4.40-9.97; p < 0.001). After adjustment for baseline knowledge, age, education, gravidity, marital status, living arrangement, reading ability, and occupation, intervention-group assignment remained significantly associated with higher post-intervention knowledge ({beta} = 5.88, 95% CI: 3.84-7.92; p < 0.001). ConclusionCulturally adapted BPCR education was associated with greater short-term improvement in knowledge than standard translated education among Hehe pregnant women. Integrating culturally and linguistically appropriate terminology, contextual explanations, and locally meaningful communication into BPCR education may strengthen knowledge outcomes. Multisite studies with stronger allocation procedures and longer follow-up are needed to confirm these findings. Trial RegistrationPan African Clinical Trials Registry: PACTR202607626025411. Registered retrospectively on 09 July 2026.

papers.title: Benchmark Self-Triage (BeST): Comparing Self-Triage Systems and Multiple Generations of OpenAI Models Against Preliminary Expert Consensus
papers.abstract: As digital self-triage becomes more widely used, quality assurance requires evaluation of both emergency recognition and overall agreement with clinical judgement, including how these outcomes differ across generations of large language models. The Benchmark Self-Triage (BeST) project intends to provide a framework to compare systems for digital self-triage against a medical 'gold standard' in Germany. As a first step in developing and demonstrating the methodology, we compared study-specific implementations of SmED 5.4.11 accessed via API and Infermedica Engine API via Microsoft Azure Healthcare Agent Service with five structured OpenAI configurations spanning multiple model generations: gpt-4.1, gpt-5.4, gpt-5.6-luna, gpt-5.6-sol, and gpt-6-astra. The manufacturers of SmED and Infermedica offer MDR-certified Class IIb triage products, but these certified products were not directly evaluated. An LLM-based patient actor covered 480 physician-curated vignettes derived from German routine triage data. A pool of seven physicians provided preliminary reference classifications and consensus for 480 vignettes. Recommendations were mapped to three urgency categories-emergency, acute, and not urgent-and evaluated using winsorised weights derived from routine triage frequencies. Weighted emergency sensitivity ranged from 51.3% (95% CI 35.5-66.3%) for gpt-4.1 to 99.9% (99.7-100.0%) for gpt-6-astra. Weighted exact three-category agreement (accuracy) ranged from 54.4% to 68.8%; gpt-4.1 achieved the highest agreement despite the lowest emergency sensitivity. No system performed best across all urgency categories. The later-generation OpenAI configurations showed a more precautionary triage profile resembling SmED, with higher sensitivity for emergency cases; gpt-6-astra showed the strongest shift. This cross-sectional comparison across model generations suggests a shift towards more precautionary triage behaviour, without establishing a longitudinal improvement in accuracy. These findings highlight the limitations of overall agreement for evaluating self-triage and support category-specific assessment. Broader expert consensus and evaluation, as well as further steps to reduce dependence on SmED-derived source data, are needed and planned before drawing conclusions about clinical safety.

papers.title: Innovations, recipients, and contexts in the implementation of pediatric neurocritical care programs: a multisite qualitative study refining i-PARIHS
papers.abstract: BackgroundPediatric neurocritical care (PNCC) has emerged as a distinct field, and many hospitals have moved to establishing dedicated PNCC programs. How practice change is implemented within these programs is not well understood. This study had two objectives. First, we sought to understand the barriers and facilitators of practice change in PNCC from the perspectives of the multiprofessional clinicians who deliver it. Second, we sought to characterize how well the integrated Promoting Action on Research Implementation in Health Services (i-PARIHS) implementation determinant framework captures them. MethodsWe conducted semi-structured interviews with a purposive sample of clinicians involved in PNCC at three U.S. academic medical centers. The interview guide was developed using i-PARIHS to organize barriers and facilitators of practice change across the innovation, recipients, context, and facilitation constructs. We applied framework analysis, combining deductive i-PARIHS, study-specific, and inductively derived categories. Two coders independently indexed the transcripts and reconciled them to consensus, with first-author adjudication. Preliminary site-level findings were validated with participants. ResultsWe interviewed 33 clinicians: 24 physicians, 7 nurses, and 2 advanced practice providers. Most determinants of practice change mapped to existing i-PARIHS constructs, but three were not adequately captured by the framework as currently specified. The most consequential was an interprofessional authority gradient that determined whose preferences prevailed when intensive care, neurology, and neurosurgery disagreed. The other two were clinician autonomy, which served as the lens through which the acceptability of a change was judged, and the affective state clinicians bring to practice change. Receptivity depended more on recipients values, prior experience, and capacity to absorb change into a demanding workflow. Facilitation was variable, frequently under-resourced, and dependent on credibility across professional groups. We translated these findings into three propositions linked to implementation strategies and outcomes. ConclusionsParticipants attributed practice change in PNCC more to the recipients of change, the multiprofessional context, and the availability of facilitation than to the strength of evidence for a given practice. i-PARIHS captured most barriers and facilitators well but may be adapted in this setting. Credible, resourced, authority-sensitive facilitation may improve the prospects for sustained practice change as institutions develop PNCC programs. Contributions to the literatureO_LIDeterminant frameworks are widely used but rarely revised once published; this study supports three i-PARIHS framework modifications potentially applicable to the general pediatric ICU and PNCC programs regarding clinician autonomy, the affective state clinicians bring to change, and the interprofessional authority gradient. C_LIO_LIWe identify authority-sensitive facilitation as an important driver of sustained practice change amongst multispecialty teams. C_LIO_LIWe offer three i-PARIHS elaborations with linked implementation outcomes and implications for selecting implementation strategies for teams with shared authority across professions. C_LI

papers.title: Researchers Behavioral Intentions to Engage in Knowledge Translation Activities and Their Association with Bibliometric Indicators: A Theory of Planned Behavior-Informed Questionnaire Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundKnowledge translation (KT) is essential for ensuring that research evidence informs policy and practice. However, little is known about researchers intentions to engage in KT activities or their relationship with conventional bibliometric indicators. This study aimed to (1) assess researchers intentions to engage in KT activities using a questionnaire informed by the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB), and (2) examine the association between these intentions and individual bibliometric indicators. MethodsA cross-sectional survey was conducted among faculty members at Tehran University of Medical Sciences. A questionnaire informed by selected constructs of the TPB was developed to assess researchers intentions to engage in activities across the seven components the action cycle of Knowledge-to-Action (KTA) framework. The instrument was validated through several rounds of expert review and then with a sample of potential participants. Bibliometric indicators (H-index, Number of Publications, Number of Citations, First-Author Publications, Corresponding Authorship, International Publications and Self-Citations) were extracted from the national academic registry. To assess representativeness, bibliometric characteristics of respondents were compared with those of a random sample of non-respondents drawn from the same registry. Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) validated the intention construct, and Structural Equation Modeling examined associations with demographic and bibliometric variables. ResultsA total of 143 researchers participated. Intention scores were highest for adapting knowledge to local contexts and identifying barriers and facilitators, and lowest for monitoring and sustaining knowledge use. CFA supported a unidimensional intention construct with favorable model-fit indicators. No bibliometric indicator was significantly associated with KT intention. Age was the only significant predictor. Respondents had stronger bibliometric profiles than non-respondents, indicating potential non-response bias. ConclusionsResearchers reported relatively strong intentions to engage in KT, but these intentions were not associated with conventional bibliometric indicators. Age was the only significant predictor. Overall, findings suggest that traditional academic metrics may not reflect KT intentions and highlight the need to strengthen institutional incentives for KT.

papers.title: Characterization of Medication-Related Errors and Prioritization of Patient-Safety Interventions in Hospital Care: A Retrospective Observational Study
papers.abstract: A. RationaleMedication-related incidents are an important patient-safety concern, particularly in critical-care and inpatient settings where polypharmacy, clinical complexity, frequent therapeutic modifications, and transitions of care increase the risk of medication errors. Systematic analysis of reported incidents can help identify predominant error patterns, potential contributing factors, and priority areas for quality improvement. The present study was undertaken to characterize medication-related incidents and identify areas requiring targeted patient-safety interventions. B. Research QuestionWhat are the predominant patterns and distribution of medication-related incidents across critical-care and inpatient units, what patient-care, process, communication, documentation, and system-level factors potentially contribute to their occurrence, and how can these findings be systematically translated into prioritized, evidence-based quality-improvement interventions to strengthen medication safety and reduce preventable medication-related harm? C. Study Design and MethodsA retrospective descriptive observational study was conducted to assess the pattern of medication-related errors identified through medication audits conducted in inpatient and critical-care settings. A total of 74 medication audit records were retrospectively reviewed. Each record was evaluated for the presence and type of medication-related error, including transcription, administration, documentation, and dispensing errors. The identified medication errors were categorized based on the nature of the error documented in the audit records. As individual records could contain more than one type of medication-related error, the error categories were considered non-mutually exclusive. Consequently, the total number of error occurrences could exceed the number of records reviewed. Descriptive statistical analysis was performed using frequency distributions and percentages to determine the relative occurrence of each medication-error category. Pareto analysis was subsequently performed to identify the predominant error categories and establish priorities for quality-improvement interventions. The Pareto analysis demonstrated that transcription and administration errors constituted the major contributors to the observed medication-related errors. The identified error patterns were further evaluated using a process-based patient-safety approach to determine potential failure points within the medication-use process. Poka-Yoke (error-proofing) principles were applied to identify opportunities for preventing or detecting errors at the point of occurrence. Based on the findings, potential interventions included standardization of medication-ordering and transcription processes, mandatory verification of medication details, strengthening of independent verification for high-alert medications, and incorporation of technology-enabled safeguards such as electronic medication administration records and barcode-based medication administration. The findings were used to identify priority areas for targeted quality-improvement interventions aimed at reducing medication-related errors and strengthening the safety and reliability of the medication-use process. D. ResultsA total of 91 medication-related error occurrences were identified across the 74 audit records reviewed. Transcription errors constituted the predominant error category (46; 50.5%), followed by administration-related errors (41; 45.1%). Documentation-related and dispensing-related errors accounted for 3 (3.3%) and 1 (1.1%) occurrences, respectively. Pareto analysis demonstrated that transcription and administration-related errors collectively accounted for 87 of the 91 identified occurrences (95.6%), indicating a substantial concentration of medication-related errors within these two categories. The cumulative frequency increased from 50.5% for transcription errors to 95.6% following inclusion of administration-related errors, while the remaining categories contributed only 4.4% of the total error occurrences. Accordingly, transcription and administration-related errors were identified as the principal priority areas for subsequent root cause analysis and quality-improvement interventions. InterpretationThe findings demonstrate that transcription errors (50.5%) and administration-related errors (45.1%) were the predominant medication-related errors, collectively accounting for 87 of the 91 identified error occurrences (95.6%). Documentation-related errors constituted 3.3%, while dispensing-related errors accounted for 1.1% of the observed occurrences. Pareto analysis revealed a marked concentration of medication-related errors within the transcription and administration domains, indicating that these two categories represented the principal areas requiring focused quality-improvement interventions. Subsequent Root Cause Analysis (RCA) and Poka-Yoke-based error-proofing approaches were therefore directed toward identifying and mitigating process vulnerabilities within these high-frequency error domains.
